The San Diego pocket mouse (Chaetodipus fallax) is a small heteromyid rodent inhabiting coastal sage scrub and chaparral communities of southern California and Baja California. Neonates emerge weighing just 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams], a diminutive birth mass that underscores the altricial condition typical of this genus. Under the thermal conditions optimal for this species, maintained at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days], a duration comparable to that reported for other Chaetodipus species of similar body size. This relatively brief intrauterine development is followed by a period of intense maternal investment, during which the altricial newborns undergo rapid somatic growth while remaining fully dependent on milk. The thermal environment appears to be physiologically optimal for gestation, as it approximates the species' preferred microhabitat temperatures within subterranean burrow systems. These burrows buffer against the extreme diurnal temperature fluctuations characteristic of chaparral ecosystems, thereby facilitating consistent embryonic development. The reproductive biology of C. fallax is thus tightly coupled to the thermal properties of its semiarid habitat.

Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition in the life cycle of Chaetodipus fallax, occurring at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C] at 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth]. By this point, the suckling juveniles have attained a wet weight of 5.5 grams [Wwx = 5.5 grams], reflecting a roughly fourfold increase from their neonatal mass. This rate of pre-weaning growth is characteristic of small-bodied heteromyids, which tend to undergo a compressed period of lactation relative to other rodent families of equivalent adult size. After weaning, the now-independent juveniles begin to consume solid seeds and insects, transitioning to the granivorous-omnivorous diet that defines the trophic niche of adult pocket mice. The precise timing of maternal provisioning cessation likely reflects an optimization between the energetic demands of lactation and the seasonal availability of high-quality forage. Field observations suggest that females may accelerate or delay weaning depending on resource abundance, though the 20-day benchmark observed under controlled thermal conditions provides a useful reference for comparative life-history analyses across Chaetodipus populations.

Sexual maturation in San Diego pocket mice follows an extended juvenile period, with puberty being attained at 166 days after birth [tp = 166 days after birth] under the standard thermal regime of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This delayed onset of reproductive capacity is noteworthy given the species' relatively small adult body mass. During the intervening months between weaning and puberty, the growing juvenile undergoes significant morphological and physiological development, ultimately reaching an ultimate wet weight of 21 grams [Wwi = 21 grams], with field-captured adults typically ranging from 17 to 22 grams. This adult body mass is consistent with other members of the fallax species group, though intraspecific variation is influenced by habitat productivity and seasonal rainfall patterns. The pubertal transition at approximately five and a half months positions young-of-the-year to enter the breeding population during the late spring or early summer, when food resources are most abundant. Such timing likely enhances the probability of successful first reproduction, as females require adequate fat reserves to sustain gestation and subsequent lactation. Fluctuating burrow temperatures experienced by wild conspecifics may accelerate or decelerate maturation rates compared to the controlled conditions of the laboratory.

Reproductive output in Chaetodipus fallax is characterized by modest litter sizes and a moderate annual frequency of breeding events. Females typically produce between 2 and 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 6 pups per litter], with the higher end of this range observed during years of exceptional precipitation and seed production. At the standard laboratory temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], females may produce up to three litters annually [F_R_i = up to three litters annually], though this maximum reproductive rate is rarely sustained in the wild due to seasonal resource constraints. The combination of moderate litter size and multiple annual reproductive events positions C. fallax as an intermediate strategist along the slow-fast life-history continuum for heteromyid rodents. This reproductive schedule imposes substantial energetic demands on lactating females, who must simultaneously maintain their own body condition while provisioning rapidly growing litters. Comparative data from sympatric Chaetodipus species suggest that litter size and frequency are plastic traits modulated by maternal age, body mass, and environmental predictability.

The basal metabolic rate of the San Diego pocket mouse, measured as resting oxygen consumption at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], is approximately 23.82 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 23.82 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic expenditure reflects the energetic costs of maintaining homeostasis within the species' preferred thermal neutral zone and is consistent with allometric predictions for a mammal of 21 grams adult body mass. Longevity records for Chaetodipus fallax, also documented at 34.7 °C, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8.3 years [am = approximately 8.3 years], a relatively extended duration for a rodent of this size and likely attributable to the predator-buffered microhabitat of underground burrows at a temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. The interplay between low basal metabolic rate, moderate reproductive output, and extended lifespan situates C. fallax as a slow-living species within the Perognathinae subfamily. Field studies incorporating mark-recapture techniques have corroborated the captive longevity estimates, with some individuals surviving more than eight years. Physiological senescence in this species appears gradual, with reproductive decline evident only in the oldest quartile of the population age structure. Collectively, these life-history traits reflect an adaptive syndrome shaped by the unpredictable rainfall patterns and variable seed production that characterize California's Mediterranean-type ecosystems.
